questions.q: What is this capstone course primarily designed to do?
options: Teach new blockchain concepts for the first time
Let students ship real, complete projects using everything taught earlier in the path
Replace the need for any earlier course in the path
Focus exclusively on blockchain theory with no code
questions.explain: This course doesn't introduce new fundamentals — it's where everything from Solidity through DeFi mechanics to testing and tooling gets applied to build three real, shippable projects.

questions.q: Why does this capstone avoid building around one fictional company, unlike some other capstones in this catalog?
options: Fictional companies are against platform policy
The student builds their own real project under their own name, so an invented company would add nothing
Blockchain projects cannot use scenario-based teaching
It was simply an arbitrary choice with no reasoning behind it
questions.explain: A capstone like this is meant to produce something genuinely the student's own — their own repo, their own project — so there's no need for (and no benefit to) an invented company narrative.

questions.q: What are this course's three flagship projects, in order?
options: A full DeFi protocol, an NFT marketplace, and a DAO governance system
A blog platform, a chat app, and a game
Three separate DeFi protocols with no variation
A DAO, then a DeFi protocol, then career prep only
questions.explain: The course builds a DeFi protocol (Project 1), an NFT marketplace (Project 2), and a DAO governance system (Project 3), followed by a career-preparation chapter.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does a GitHub profile with 2-3 deep, complete projects usually serve a job search better than one with many shallow projects?
options: Hiring teams evaluating real engineering ability look for depth — architecture, tests, and tradeoffs — that shallow projects rarely show
Recruiters only count the number of repositories
Shallow projects always compile faster
Job applications require exactly three projects by industry standard
questions.explain: Depth — clear architecture, tests, documented tradeoffs — is what interviewers actually probe for; a long list of unfinished repos signals breadth without substance.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed in this lesson as part of what makes a project "complete"?
options: Tests that include fuzz and invariant checks, not just the happy path
A frontend that reads live on-chain state rather than a disconnected copy
A verified testnet deployment with a linkable address
A minimum of 1,000 GitHub stars on the repository
questions.explain: The lesson's five completeness criteria are commented contracts, tests beyond the happy path, a live-reading frontend, a verified testnet deployment, and a README explaining tradeoffs — star counts are never mentioned as a requirement.
